title: LiteratureSearch
description: Shape contract for the literature pass: a written note in, and the handful of concepts worth looking up in PubMed out. Not an answer to a clinical question and not a summary — a list of search topics, each tied to the line of the note it came from.

x-notes.whatThisTaskIsFor: The topics this task emits are resolved against NCBI's MeSH vocabulary and then combined into a PubMed query by the consuming application. The model therefore chooses WHAT to look up and never how: it does not write query syntax, does not name MeSH descriptors, and does not see a result. A model asked for descriptors emits plausible ones that are not in the vocabulary — `Heart Failure, Preserved Ejection Fraction` reads like a descriptor, is not one, and returns zero results, which is indistinguishable from a gap in the literature. Asking for ordinary English words moves that failure to a lookup that can say 'no such descriptor' out loud.
x-notes.sourceIsAQuote: `source` is a span of the note copied character by character, and the application verifies it by literal search under the pack's [clinical.quoteVerification] rule — the same check the note items themselves go through. A topic whose source is not in the note is DISCARDED. This is what stands between a search and a fabrication: without it, a model that invented a condition would send that condition to a third party and hand the clinician a page of papers about a disease nobody has.
x-notes.termIsTranslatedAndSourceIsNot: MeSH is an English vocabulary, so `term` is English whatever the note's language. `source` is a copy and is never translated: a Spanish note produces a Spanish source and an English term, and the pair is what makes the translation inspectable. It also means `term` is NOT verifiable against the note, which is the honest limit of this contract — the check says the topic came from a line of this note, not that the English is a faithful rendering of it.
x-notes.propertyOrder: LOAD-BEARING, as in every schema in this pack: llama.cpp compiles properties into the grammar in the order given. `source` is emitted BEFORE `term` so the model has to find a line of the note before it names a concept. Reversed, the field would be a citation written after the fact for something already decided, which is how a plausible topic acquires evidence it never had.
x-notes.emptyIsAnAnswer: `topics: []` is correct and expected. Most routine consultations contain no question worth a literature search, and a grammar that forced at least one topic would make padding the only legal reply — which is the failure mode that ends with a clinician ignoring the panel entirely.
x-notes.cap3: Three topics, because PubMed combines them with AND. A fourth leg narrows a search that is already narrow, and the difference between three and four is usually the difference between a short page of results and an empty one. It is a bound on a query rather than a judgement about how interesting a consultation can be.
x-notes.evidenceIsClosed: A closed enum rather than free text because it is compiled into a publication-type filter downstream. PubMed does not reject an unknown publication type — it returns zero results, which reads exactly like a literature gap. `any` is a real answer and the prompt says so.

topics.description: The concepts worth looking up, at most three, most important first. An empty array is the correct answer for a note that contains no question.

evidence.description: What kind of paper would answer the question this note raises. 'any' when you cannot tell, or when the note raises more than one kind.

topic.description: One thing to look up, and the line of the note it comes from.

source.description: The line of the note this topic comes from, copied character by character. Never translated, never reworded. A source that cannot be found in the note discards the topic.

term.description: The concept in ENGLISH, as a clinician would name it in an index: 'heart failure', 'empagliflozin', 'atrial fibrillation'. No dose, no frequency, no brand, no query syntax.
